title: How to invest in REIT ETFs for real estate exposure without buying property
description: A guide to Equity REITs, Mortgage REITs, and the tax implications of passive real estate.
content:
For decades, 'investing in real estate' meant fixing toilets, chasing tenants for rent, and taking on massive mortgage debt. The Real Estate Investment Trust (REIT) changed the game. REITs allow you to own slices of massive commercial empires—skyscrapers in NYC, data centers in Virginia, and cell towers across the Midwest—without ever leaving your couch. By buying REIT ETFs, you get the inflation-hedging benefits of real estate and the high dividend income, all with the liquidity of a stock. This guide explains how to add this powerful asset class to your portfolio.

Key Takeaways

  • The 'Pass-Through' Structure: By law, REITs must pay out 90% of their taxable income to shareholders as dividends. This results in yields often 2x-3x higher than the S&P 500.
  • Equity vs. Mortgage: Equity REITs own buildings (safer, growth-focused). Mortgage REITs own loans (riskier, yield-focused). Beginners should stick to Equity REITs.
  • Tax Inefficiency: REIT dividends are usually 'Non-Qualified,' meaning they are taxed at your full ordinary income tax rate. They are best held in an IRA.
  • Uncorrelated Returns: Real estate often zigs when tech stocks zag, lowering overall portfolio volatility.

Why It Matters (US Context)

The US REIT market is the largest and most liquid in the world. It includes unique sectors like 'Data Center REITs' (powering AI) and 'Tower REITs' (powering 5G). Buying a broad US Real Estate ETF gives you exposure to the physical infrastructure of the American economy.

Top REIT ETFs Compared

Don't try to pick the single winning mall operator. Buy the sector.

1. Vanguard Real Estate ETF (VNQ)

  • Focus: Broad Market (Residential, Industrial, Retail, Health).
  • Yield: ~4.0%.
  • Expense Ratio: 0.12%.
  • Verdict: The default choice. It owns everything.

2. Schwab US REIT ETF (SCHH)

  • Focus: Similar to VNQ but excludes some specialty sectors (like timber/towers).
  • Yield: ~3.5%.
  • Expense Ratio: 0.07%.
  • Verdict: Slightly cheaper, slightly less diversified.

3. Realty Income (O) - *Individual Stock Exception*

Known as 'The Monthly Dividend Company'. It is not an ETF, but it is so diversified (owning 13,000+ properties like 7-Elevens and Walgreens) that many investors treat it like a fund. It has paid 600+ consecutive monthly dividends.

How to Allocate

  1. The 10% Limit: Real Estate is a sector, not the whole market. Limit REITs to 5-10% of your total portfolio. If you own VTI (Total Stock Market), you already own ~3% REITs inside it.
  2. Asset Location: Put VNQ in your Roth IRA. The high dividends will compound tax-free. If you put it in a taxable account, you lose ~30% of the dividend to taxes every year.
  3. Avoid mREITs: Mortgage REITs (like NLY) offer 12% yields but are incredibly sensitive to interest rates and often lose share price value. They are yield traps for beginners.

Frequently Asked Questions

Is a REIT better than a rental property?

It is different. Rental properties offer leverage (mortgages) and tax breaks (depreciation) that REITs don't. But REITs offer zero work and instant liquidity. For passive investors, REITs win.

Do REITs protect against inflation?

Yes. Property owners raise rents when inflation is high. This flows through to the dividend. It is a natural hedge.

Why did REITs crash in 2022?

Rising interest rates hurt real estate (borrowing costs go up). However, now that rates have stabilized, REIT valuations look attractive compared to expensive tech stocks.
